06-M2.verdict_why: No source tests the exact rule (a tutor that never opens itself and never offers help unprompted), but adjacent evidence conflicts. Backing the wait-only design: in a classroom ITS, students who restrained themselves from requesting help (keeping-off) achieved greater learning gains (c3), and a review plus the Help Tutor work treat on-demand help as the appropriate baseline that students should use deliberately (c1, c14). Cutting against it: help avoidance when help is needed predicted worse robust learning (c11), unsolicited "Assertions" significantly raised unsolicited hint usage and showed an aptitude-treatment interaction with prior proficiency (c12), and effective human one-to-one math tutors gave hints more frequently and proactively than less effective ones (c8). Evidence on tutoring help-seeking itself is mixed: feedback improved deliberate help use but not domain learning outcomes (c14), so several converging sources are needed before claiming strong support either way.
06-M2.code_vs_evidence: The rule matches the tradition of on-demand help in ITSs (c1, c14 recommend including on-demand help) and one classroom study suggesting restraint can pay off (c3). But the evidence is not one-sided: c11 and c12 show that some students who need help never ask, and that unsolicited, well-designed hints can increase hint use and aid low-prior-proficiency students, while c8 shows more effective human tutors hint more proactively. Gap: none of these studies randomizes the precise rule the app implements (always silent until asked; no proactive offer), so the mechanism as specified is a design choice rather than a directly tested intervention. A defensible design would keep learner-initiated help as the default but add carefully designed unsolicited support (e.g., Assertions) after inactivity, especially for low-prior-knowledge learners, and note that help-seeking training improved deliberate help use without improving domain learning (c14). The one candidate whose title poses the exact question (Razzaq, "Hints: Is It Better to Give or Wait to Be Asked?") is available only as a title, so no evidence could be extracted from it.

06-M3.verdict_why: Several meta-analyses converge that testing without help aids long-term retention (c1, c2), one large field experiment shows unguarded generative-AI access harms later unaided performance (c10), and validity literature backs the need for unaided assessment (c23). However, no retrieved source tests the exact page-path rule, and boundary findings conflict with a blanket retrieval claim: the testing effect was not robust for mathematics (c5) and retrieval practice impaired transitive inference (c3). Convergence is on the general principles, not the specific rule.
06-M3.code_vs_evidence: Partly matched. The general principles line up: retrieval sitting without help is supported for retention (c1, c2), and c10 is direct causal evidence that unguarded AI access during practice can harm later unaided performance, backing the app's decision to withhold the full tutor on assessment pages while c23 supports why an aided test would not measure knowledge. Gaps: (1) no source studies the app's exact rule of switching tutor mode by page path, so the specific tiering (method-only on placements, stage checks, retention enforcer, review, etc. versus full elsewhere) is a design choice not directly validated; (2) c10 tested full access versus a safeguarded tutor, not literally 'method-only, never confirms an answer', so the precise safeguard design is untested; (3) the retrieval benefit is domain- and task-dependent (not robust in math, negative for inference), so enforcing retrieval-only on every listed page may not always help and could even hinder certain complex skills; (4) c10's population is high school mathematics, so generalization to this app's learners and subject matter is uncertain, and its correlation-like survey neighbors (c14, c15) do not support causal claims.

06-M4.verdict_why: Evidence converges that unfettered answer-giving is risky (a large field experiment found unrestricted GPT-4 access harmed later performance while safeguards mitigated it, c29) and that directly obtaining answers via gaming predicts lower post-test scores (c1), with generation/self-explanation and ICAP theory favoring active construction over passive reception (c4). Against this, bottom-out hints/answers are not uniformly harmful — some use acts as worked examples (c5) and a scaffolding chatbot matched traditional hints with no learning difference and even lowered confidence (c26). No study tests this exact rule ("no rule against giving the answer" on practice pages), so it is partly a design choice; the principles conflict rather than fully settle it.
06-M4.code_vs_evidence: The app's rule leans toward the "unrestricted" condition that the strongest study (c29) found can harm learning, since it deliberately places no rule against giving answers on practice pages. This runs against the guardrail/gaming/generation evidence (c29, c1, c4, c30) that suggests withholding or structuring assistance protects learning. It is partially supported by c5 and c26, which show answer-level help is not always harmful and depends on how it is used. Gap: no peer-reviewed study isolates this exact design decision, so the rule is largely a design choice supported only indirectly; the app should watch whether full mode invites answer-copying/gaming (c1) versus productive worked-example use (c5), and consider that giving answers may reduce later confidence (c26).

06-M5.verdict_why: No source tests the app's exact rule (2-4 short sentences ending in one question or next step). The underlying principles are well supported: interactive/constructive dialogue and prompting (Chi 2001; Chi 2014 ICAP; Sailer 2024 meta-analysis), questioning and collaborative dialogue (Graesser 1995), and chunking into small learner-paced segments (Mayer 2005, median d = 0.98). One experimental study (Engelmann 2022) found interactive vs constructive made no difference for a specific content domain, so the general principle is not universal. Because the specific reply-shape rule was never tested, this is a design choice grounded in general evidence rather than a directly validated rule.
06-M5.code_vs_evidence: The 2-4 sentence length and learner-facing question loosely match the segmenting principle and interactive/constructive dialogue evidence, but no study operationalizes reply shape that way, and the mapping of "short sentences" to "learner-paced segments" is an analogy, not a tested equivalence. The "one question or concrete next step" rule is consistent with prompting/interactive dialogue findings but not directly measured as a per-turn design constraint. Gap: (a) no direct evidence on sentence count or always ending with a question, (b) Engelmann 2022 shows interactive-vs-constructive effects can be null depending on content, so the rule may not generalize across all subjects, and (c) Chi 2001 notes benefits were limited by students' reading abilities — an individual-difference boundary condition the fixed reply shape ignores.

06-M9.verdict_why: The general principle is well supported: reviews and meta-analyses converge that contingent, step-level scaffolding tied to the learner's current state is effective (VanLehn 2006; van de Pol 2010, 2013; Doo 2020, and similarly Kim 2017, Belland 2017). But two sources cut against the strong version of the specific claims: VanLehn (2011) did not confirm that finer interaction granularity (i.e., step-level hints over answer-based) is more effective, and van de Pol (2018) found contingency of teacher support did not affect students' uptake or answer accuracy. No source tests the exact app rule of surfacing the question/passage/choices (without answer key) plus the learner's pick/typing, so that specific rule is a design choice inferred from general principles.
06-M9.code_vs_evidence: The app's rule matches the broad evidence that tutors should see the learner's current step-level work and state to diagnose errors and give contingent, context-sensitive help (c2, c3, c8, c4). It goes beyond what is directly tested: the exact choice to show the learner's copy of question, passage and choices minus the answer key is not studied, and the claims that step-level/context-sensitive hints beat general help and that contingency alone improves outcomes are challenged (c11 did not confirm the granularity belief; c20 found contingency did not affect uptake or accuracy). Showing the learner's own copy without an answer key is a defensible design choice (it preserves diagnosis while avoiding leaking answers), but the app should not claim that step-level page awareness by itself guarantees better outcomes; the evidence supports contingent diagnosis, not the display rule itself.

06-M10.verdict_why: Two controlled experiments (c2, c4) converge on modality equivalence: spoken dialogue does not beat typed input and is worse for highly motivated learners, so the implicit spoken-advantage assumption is not supported. Speech-recognition error evidence is ambivalent: errors were unrelated to learning gains but linked to tutor evaluations (c2), while non-native speech forced heavy adaptation (c9). The specific one-to-three-sentence spoken-reply rule has no direct study, so that part is a design choice.
06-M10.code_vs_evidence: Push-to-talk plus spoken replies is broadly consistent with evidence that spoken and typed tutoring deliver equivalent gains (c2, c4) and that ASR-based tutors can improve outcomes (c19). But the app's implication that voice mode helps learning is not supported: spoken was on par, and typing was better for motivated learners (c4). Speech input is error-prone; c2 links recognition errors to lower tutor evaluations (not lower learning) and c9 says non-native speech demands many adaptations. No source tests the one-to-three-sentence reply limit, TTS spoken output with visuals, or whether a paid better voice ($5 ledger) improves learning. Gaps: reply-length rule and voice-quality tier are unevidenced design choices.

06-M11.verdict_why: No source tests the app's exact rule (last 14 turns verbatim, fold to a ~120-word summary, quote up to 4 earlier turns). The general principles are backed: a scoping review finds memory/consistency a recurring rapport lever (c16), and OLM work shows persistent, negotiated learner models support planning, reflection and model maintenance across time (c1, c4, c6, c8). But the support is conceptual, review-level or non-experimental, and even the SPA evidence base is dominated by short single-session experiments, so cross-session summarization is not directly validated. One design paper (c3) adds a caution about model accuracy.
06-M11.code_vs_evidence: Match on the general principle, gap on the specifics. Persisting and re-surfacing learner information across sessions (and, per c16, memory/consistency for rapport) is consistent with the evidence; the concrete numbers — a 14-turn verbatim window, a ~120-word summary threshold, and quoting up to 4 turns — are untested design choices. No study addresses the summarization window size or the verbatim-vs-summary trade-off, so these thresholds should be framed as tunable defaults, not evidence-based constants. The after-state (c16 review) also notes short single-session experiments predominate, leaving cross-session retention of rapport only indirectly supported.

06-M12.verdict_why: No study tests the exact app rule of labelling page and learner text as "notes"; it is a specific implementation of the broader, well-supported principle of separating instructions from data. That principle is backed by converging security sources (Greshake's data/instruction blurring, OWASP LLM01, role-separated prompting in LocalAlign, and Milani's education-context cases), while other sources show that prompt-level separation alone is not a guarantee.
06-M12.code_vs_evidence: The design matches the general evidence: treating retrieved/page text and learner messages as content rather than instructions aligns with the widely documented cause of indirect prompt injection (c1, c18) and with defenses that segregate trusted instructions from untrusted input (c17, c10, c9). The gap is the strength of the guarantee: the app's phrasing that such text "cannot change the tutor's rules" overstates what prompt-level labelling can deliver, since system-prompt-only separation fails under evasion (c11) and the same defense prompt can even increase attack success for some models (c5), and defenses can lower utility (c13). Evidence-based practice would add defense-in-depth (provenance/privilege separation, output filtering, human sign-off) rather than rely on labelling alone.

06-M13.verdict_why: Converging evidence supports the general principle: an RCT (Kestin) and a 35-study meta-analysis (Wu) find LLM/ChatGPT tutoring improves outcomes, and a large high-school field experiment (Bastani) shows pedagogical guardrails preserve learning while plain ChatGPT access can harm it. But the evidence is not unanimous: a meta-analysis of RCTs (Che) found large language models no better than traditional instruction in clinical simulation, and the specific rule here (a general-purpose dock served through an approved provider chain) has not itself been trialled. Hence moderate rather than strong.
06-M13.code_vs_evidence: Partly matches. The design is right to route answers through a controlled provider chain and its concern about hallucination is well-founded (Huang; More shows guardrails/RAG can cut hallucinated content by 30–45%). The gap: the dock is described as general-purpose, whereas the strongest evidence (Bastani) shows that unfettered general chat can degrade learning and that safeguard prompts are what mitigate harm; sources also note limits of guardrails (hallucination reduced, not eliminated; prompting/threshold effects). No trial tests this exact general-purpose-dock-with-guardrails configuration, so the app's rule extrapolates from the general principle.

06-M1.verdict_why: Bloom (1984), VanLehn (2011) and Kulik (2015) converge on tutoring and intelligent tutoring improving learning over conventional/no tutoring, which backs the general principle. But the evidence conflicts on the on-demand, learner-initiated element: Steenbergen-Hu's K–12 math meta-analysis found ITS effects near zero (g = 0.01–0.09), and Aleven's work shows learners underuse on-demand help and that improving help-seeking behaviour did not raise learning outcomes. So tutoring access helps, but the specific passive-button mechanism is not clearly supported.
06-M1.code_vs_evidence: The app's rule—an opt-in, non-interrupting tutor button on every page—matches the general principle that tutoring and ITS can raise achievement. Its weakest link is the on-demand, learner-initiated feature: evidence indicates learners do not seek help effectively or when they need it, so a purely passive button may go unused, and prompts to improve help-seeking improved behaviour but not outcomes. Gaps: no study tests a persistent per-page button specifically; ITS effects depend on subject, duration, test alignment and implementation quality; and the non-interrupting design may conflict with the finding that learners rarely initiate help voluntarily.

06-M6.verdict_why: Converging sources back the general principles behind this block: knowledge-state modeling (Corbett 1994), adaptation to skill proficiency/review of adaptive feedback (Leyzberg 2018; Bimba 2017), personalized feedback (Kochmar 2021), and misconception/error-targeted feedback (Qian 2019; Shute 2008's call for specific, timely feedback). But no source tests the app's exact rule — a ~900-token block with a fixed priority order that cuts later sections first. That specific budgeting and ordering is an engineering decision, not an evidence-derived one, and Hattie (2007) cautions that feedback type and delivery can be differentially effective or even harmful.
06-M6.code_vs_evidence: Direction matches the evidence: adapting to mastery/weak skills and targeting a learner's specific misconceptions/errors is supported by reviews and studies. Gaps: (1) nothing tests the token budget or the priority order (e.g., page and on-screen content ranked above mastery and misconceptions); (2) Shute stresses feedback should be specific and timely — a large combined block risks diluting specificity; (3) treating misconceptions as stable listed items may oversimplify them (dynamic-systems views, Svoboda 2023, argue misconceptions emerge situationally rather than being held or not held). The model's contents are plausible but the exact packaging is unverified.

06-M7.verdict_why: Several converging studies support the general principle: a randomized experiment (Córdova) found personalization raised motivation, engagement and learning, a randomized ITS experiment (Walkington 2013) found faster, more accurate problem solving, and a large quasi-experiment (Awofala) found higher motivation. But the evidence conflicts on achievement: a within-subject study (Bates) found no significant achievement gain, and Bernacki explicitly questions whether personalization improves both interest and achievement and whether situational interest is the mechanism. Effects also appear concentrated in specific skills and in struggling students rather than uniformly. So this is not a settled 'strong' case.
06-M7.code_vs_evidence: The app's rule — feeding the learner's own typed interests to the tutor so it draws examples from them — matches the tested principle of context personalization, and studies did use student-supplied interests (interest inventories / self-selected topics), so the mechanism is well aligned. The match is moderate: evidence is strongest for motivation and situational interest, and for performance on some math skills or among struggling students, but at least one study found no achievement benefit. Gap: no cited study tests the exact rule (a chat tutor generating examples from interests typed in onboarding), and most effects come from math word problems in tutoring systems, so claims that this raise 'performance and learning' generally would overstate what the sources show.

06-M8.verdict_why: The negative half of the rule (never telling the tutor a VAK/visual-auditory-kinesthetic style) is strongly backed: multiple reviews and experiments converge that the meshing hypothesis lacks evidence (Rogowsky 2014; Aslaksen 2018), and surveys show the myth is widespread among teachers and academics (Dekker 2012; Newton 2017). The positive half — feeding the tutor a scorecard of measured study behaviour — is a design choice with no study of this exact rule; Dinsmore (2022) supports the general principle of basing instruction on measured knowledge, strategies and interest, but the specific scorecard-in-tutor mechanism is untested. One theoretical review (Awla 2014) argues matching styles does improve achievement, a dissenting view the experimental and review evidence does not support.
06-M8.code_vs_evidence: Matches the evidence for the "never a learning-style type" rule: the strongest sources (reviews and a controlled experiment) find no support for matching instruction to style preference, and the myth is documented as widespread among educators, including the dissent (Awla 2014) which the better evidence does not back. The "adapt to measured study behaviour" rule is only indirectly supported: Dinsmore (2022) endorses building instruction on measured knowledge/strategies/interest, but no picked source tests showing an LLM tutor a learner's measured scorecard, so the exact rule is a design choice. Gap: no study of the app's specific behaviour-level adaptation, and Dinsmore's variables are not identical to a session-derived study-behaviour scorecard.
